clue.text: Irritate good number in party

parts.note: to get to someone is to annoy them
G is the standard abbreviation for good
read as 'numb-er', something that numbs, as an anaesthetic does

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed by a fine turnout at a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is a crossword favourite: read it as numb-er, a thing that numbs, so an anaesthetic such as ETHER.
explanation.definitionFit: A get-together is an informal social gathering, which is exactly what a casual party is.

clue.text: Studio artist clearly explained symbol in browser

parts.note: graphic means vividly and explicitly described

indicators.note: one item placed in another sits inside it, so the symbol goes within the browser

parts.note: a deer browses on leaves and shoots, so it is a browser
a sign is a symbol

explanation.surface: An artist in a studio explains clearly what an icon in a web browser means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browser' points at web software, but here it is an animal that grazes on shrubs and leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A graphic designer is a commercial artist who typically works in a design studio producing layouts and visuals.

clue.text: Half-hearted course director who does high-level work?

indicators.note: with only half its heart left, the word loses one of its two central letters

parts.note: a tiller steers a boat, directing its course

explanation.surface: A lukewarm course leader is wondered about as someone doing important senior work.
explanation.walkthrough: The centre of the steering word is a double L; dropping one of the pair halves its heart. 'High-level' is literal: the worker is up on the roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiler lays tiles on roofs, so the job is literally carried out at a height, which the question mark flags.

clue.text: Former head is dear chap

parts.note: old as in previous, one-time
bean is slang for the head

explanation.surface: An ex-headteacher turns out to be a lovely fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former head' reads as a retired principal, but it is two pieces: bean is old slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Old bean is a dated, affectionate British form of address between men, much like 'my dear fellow'.

clue.text: Message from exhausted servant in English stately home

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: the servant ends up placed inside the grand house

parts.note: a pile is a large imposing house

indicators.note: an exhausted word is emptied out, leaving just its outside letters

parts.note: only the first and last letters remain

explanation.surface: A note sent by a worn-out butler in an English country mansion.
explanation.walkthrough: A pile is informal British for a grand country house.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a letter, especially a formal or literary one, so it is a written message.

clue.text: Dubious relations restrained by man's social worker

indicators.note: something restrained is held in, so it sits inside what holds it

parts.note: he's, the man is
it is slang for sexual relations
ants live in colonies and are workers, so a social insect

explanation.surface: Questionable family members are kept in check by a man's caseworker.
explanation.walkthrough: Social worker is not a council employee but an insect living in colonies; 'it' is old slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubious can mean doubtful or unsure in mind, and someone hesitant is uncertain and reluctant to commit.

clue.text: Petitions European parliament initially to object to food banks

indicators.note: banks line both sides, so the outer word flanks the rest like a riverbank

parts.note: to resent something is to object to it

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the two words before it

parts.note: first letter
first letter
rations, the food allowance, opening letter of its wrapper
rest of rations, the food allowance

explanation.surface: Members of the European parliament lodge complaints opposing food banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food banks' reads as charity, but banks is the container signal: RATIONS surrounds E, P and RESENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Representations are formal statements of a case or protest made to an authority, much like petitions.

clue.text: Pay compensation for person who pulls round

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: one who draws, as in drawing a cart or a pint

explanation.surface: Payment for someone who tows a vehicle back on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulls round' suggests a recovery, but round is the turnaround signal acting on the puller.
explanation.definitionFit: To reward someone is to give them something in return for their effort or service, recompensing them.

clue.text: Bill is right taking Dawn's name

indicators.note: the letter for right takes the spot that the abbreviation for name occupied

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
an advent is a coming or dawn of something new
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A man called Bill assumes a woman's name, Dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitals make Bill and Dawn look like people; dawn here means a beginning. R replaces N in ADVENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a printed public notice or poster, and an advert is an advertisement, such as one posted on a wall.

clue.text: Gave opportunities to skilled objective nurses

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, as a baby is nursed in the arms

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal
able means capable, competent

explanation.surface: A hospital department where the goal of capable nurses was to give people chances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' looks like a profession, but it is the verb: END holds ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To enable someone is to give them the means or chance to do something, so it is giving opportunities.

clue.text: Popular drink I had is flavourless

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular
a sip is a small drink
contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A popular beverage that I tried turned out to be bland.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid describes food or drink lacking taste, bland and with no strong flavour.

clue.text: Revolting crime cases assigned to officer repulse novelist

parts.note: ABH is actual bodily harm, a criminal offence in English law

indicators.note: a case is an outer covering, so only the outside letters of each following word are used

parts.note: first and last letters
first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: An officer assigned to a crime finds a novelist repulsive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' looks like the noun after crime, but it signals the outside letters of officer, repulse and novelist. ABH is actual bodily harm, an assault charge in UK law.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abhorrent inspires disgust and loathing, so it is revolting in the sense of repugnant.

clue.text: Subject of interest finally released by police

indicators.note: something released by a captor is let go, so it leaves the word holding it

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: A person of interest is let go at last by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person of interest' is police jargon, but here interest only supplies its final letter, which drops off THE MET. The Met is London's police force.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the main topic or subject of a talk, a piece of writing or a work of art.

clue.text: Reduce the length of court's enclosure

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to cut short, as an animal's tail is cut
second meaning: the railed box where a defendant stands in a criminal court

explanation.surface: Shortening a courtroom pen.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to shorten or cut, as of tails or wages; the noun is the defendant's railed area in a courtroom.

clue.text: Trainee satisfied about new prisoner's condition

parts.note: an intern is a trainee on a work placement

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: met as in fulfilled, demands met
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A junior employee content with how a new inmate is doing.
explanation.definitionFit: Internment is confinement without trial, typically in wartime, which is the state a detainee is held in.

clue.text: Retreat from reality somehow beginning to create impasse

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are assembled in a new order
the beginning of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Running away from real life somehow leads to deadlock.
explanation.definitionFit: Escapism is seeking distraction from unpleasant realities, typically through fantasy or entertainment, a mental retreat.

clue.text: Material witness who's easily taken in

parts.note: a seer is one who sees, an onlooker
a sucker is a gullible person

explanation.surface: Important evidence from a gullible witness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material witness' is a legal phrase, but material is the definition, a fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Seersucker is a thin puckered cotton fabric, often striped, used for summer clothing, so a material.

clue.text: Rescue suspect in custody?

indicators.note: something suspect is dodgy or not right, so the letters are out of their proper order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Free the suspect being held by police?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as the person held, but it is the signal to rearrange the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Secure can mean safely locked up or held fast, and a prisoner in custody is securely detained; the question mark marks the stretch.

clue.text: Consumer champion introduces con artist

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for champion, as in dog shows
one who consumes food

explanation.surface: A consumer rights campaigner presents a fraudster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumer champion' reads as one campaigner, but the two words split, and the champion comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheater is a person who deceives or defrauds others, which is what a swindling con artist does.

clue.text: Leave out Times Crossword's first boring puzzle

indicators.note: boring as in drilling into, so these letters bore their way inside

parts.note: elude, to baffle, opening letter
X is the multiplication sign, times

indicators.note: first points at the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: first letter
rest of elude, to baffle

explanation.surface: Skip the Times crossword's first clue because the puzzle is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T makes Times the newspaper; it is the multiplication sign. X and C bore into ELUDE, to baffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To exclude something is to omit it or keep it out, which is what leaving it out means.

clue.text: Attempt to make point stick

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a go or try, as in having a go
second meaning: to thrust a sharp point into something

explanation.surface: Trying to get one's argument to land.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a try at something; the verb means to pierce with a pointed blade, driving the tip in.

clue.text: Purchase some paper reportedly for ancient craft

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: a ream is a quantity of paper, 500 sheets

explanation.surface: Buying stationery, by all accounts, to make a model of an old boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient craft' could be a trade or skill, but it is a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A bireme was an ancient galley with two banks of oars, used by the Greeks, Phoenicians and Romans.

clue.text: Friend from London joins church in America

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church; that the three words also run the letters together is a coincidence of the charade
taken as written
A is the abbreviation for America

explanation.surface: A London pal goes to a church in the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang: china plate rhymes with mate.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang, 'china plate' stands for mate, so a Londoner's china is a pal or friend.

clue.text: Opposing leaders of enemy nations first meeting

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so the opening letter of each following word is taken

parts.note: first letter
first letter
counter means opposing, contrary

explanation.surface: Heads of rival countries come face to face for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' tells you the leading letters go before the word for opposing.
explanation.definitionFit: An encounter is a meeting, especially an unexpected or hostile one, between people or forces.

clue.text: Join train on return journey, avoiding terminals

indicators.note: a return journey goes back the way it came, so the word runs backwards
terminals are the stations at each end, so both end letters are skipped

parts.note: a train of attendants is a retinue

explanation.surface: Catch a train coming back, skipping the end stations.
explanation.walkthrough: The railway imagery is all misdirection: a train is a procession of followers. Strip its ends, then run it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To unite is to bring or come together, combining into one, which is what joining does.

clue.text: Destroy corruption after one's moved to act without restraint

indicators.note: moving the one puts it into a fresh place in the other word
once the one has been moved, it is no longer where it was

parts.note: to ruin is to wreck
rot is decay, moral or physical

explanation.surface: Wrecking a corrupt system after someone has shifted, to run amok.
explanation.walkthrough: One is I, the roman numeral: it leaves RUIN and slips into ROT.
explanation.definitionFit: To run riot is to behave in a wild, unrestrained, disorderly way, out of control.

clue.text: Constant habit?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unchanging, the same throughout
second meaning: a habit is a monk's or nun's garment, a set outfit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Constant habit' sounds like a routine one never breaks; habit is also clothing, like a nun's dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniform as an adjective means unvarying; as a noun it is standard prescribed dress, as a religious habit is.

clue.text: Cruel engineers in need of inspector?

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers
Inspector Morse, the Oxford TV detective
-less means lacking

explanation.surface: Harsh mechanics who could do with an inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is a British TV detective; RE are the army's Royal Engineers. Being in need of Morse leaves you Morse-less.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorseless means without pity or compassion, relentless, which makes it a synonym for cruel.
